To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the addition of salt to polyelectrolys decomplexates them via a zipper mechanism driven by charge correlation and water binding capability, and that the addition of divalent salt is much more effective than monovalemt salt.
the addition of salt to a DNA/polylysine complex causes a gradual, zipper-like decomplexation driven by the formation of charge correlations between the DNA and polylysines.
polyelectroleyte complexation and decomplexation are driven by charge correlations and ion chemistry.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the understanding of the molecular mechanism of the decomplexation of a polyelectroylete (polylysine) and a polyanion (DNA) in aqueous solution, and the effect of salt concentration on this process.
the fundamental properties of polyelecto-lytes and their interactions with ions and water, and how these properties can be exploited to control the behavior of polyelectolytes.

the understanding of the molecular mechanisms of polyelectlyte complex decomplexation and dissociation, and how the addition of salt can affect the stability of the complex, and the release rate of the polyelectrolys.

the decomplexation process is a charge correlation driven zipper-like mechanism in which the water molecules are involved in the process and the salt ions are involved in the charge correlations and water structure.

the complex between DNA and Polylysine is destabilized and spontaneously opens in a gradual, charge correlation driven zipper-like mechanism.
